options.how_it_arises: Differentiated the outer cosine function to $-\sin(x^3)$ but forgot to multiply by the derivative of the inner function $x^3$.
options.feedback: You differentiated the outer cosine function correctly, but forgot to multiply by the derivative of $x^3$. Multiplying by $3x^2$ gives $-3x^2 \sin(x^3)$.
Correct! Applying the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{du}[\cos(u)] \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[x^3] = -\sin(x^3) \cdot 3x^2 = -3x^2 \sin(x^3)$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated the inner function $x^3$ to $3x^2$, but left the outer cosine function undifferentiated.
options.feedback: You differentiated the inner term $x^3$ to get $3x^2$, but kept the outer cosine function unchanged. Make sure to also differentiate $\cos(u)$ to $-\sin(u)$, giving $-3x^2 \sin(x^3)$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated $\cos(u)$ as $\sin(u)$ instead of $-\sin(u)$, dropping the minus sign.
options.feedback: You set up the chain rule properly, but dropped the minus sign when differentiating cosine. Remember that $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos(x)] = -\sin(x)$, so the result is $-3x^2 \sin(x^3)$.

questions.solution: Let $y = \cos(x^3)$ and $u = x^3$. Then $y = \cos(u)$. By the chain rule, $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = -\sin(u) \cdot (3x^2) = -3x^2 \sin(x^3)$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated the inner function $3x^2$ to $6x$, but left the outer function $\tan(\cdot)$ undifferentiated.
options.feedback: You calculated the derivative of the inner term $3x^2$ as $6x$, but left the outer $\tan(\cdot)$ untouched. Differentiate $\tan(u)$ to $\sec^2(u)$ to get $6x \sec^2(3x^2)$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated the outer tangent function to $\sec^2(3x^2)$ but forgot to multiply by the derivative of $3x^2$.
options.feedback: You differentiated the tangent function correctly, but forgot to multiply by the derivative of the inner function $3x^2$. Multiply by $6x$ to get $6x \sec^2(3x^2)$.
Correct! Differentiating the outer function gives $\sec^2(3x^2)$ and multiplying by the inner derivative $6x$ yields $6x \sec^2(3x^2)$.

options.how_it_arises: Treated $\tan(3x^2)$ as a product $\tan(x) \cdot 3x^2$ and differentiated $3x^2$ to $6x$.
options.feedback: You treated $\tan(3x^2)$ as a multiplication of two separate terms instead of a composite function. Use the chain rule on the inner argument $3x^2$ to get $6x \sec^2(3x^2)$.

questions.solution: Let $y = \tan(3x^2)$ and $u = 3x^2$. Then $y = \tan(u)$. By the chain rule, $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = \sec^2(u) \cdot (6x) = 6x \sec^2(3x^2)$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated $e^u$ and $\cos(v)$, but stopped one layer early and forgot to multiply by the derivative of $3x$.
options.feedback: You differentiated the exponential and cosine layers correctly, but stopped one layer early. Don't forget to multiply by the derivative of the innermost term $3x$, which is $3$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated $\cos(3x)$ as $\sin(3x)$, forgetting the negative sign.
options.feedback: You differentiated all three layers using the chain rule, but forgot the negative sign when taking the derivative of cosine. Since $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos(x)] = -\sin(x)$, the answer is $-3\sin(3x) e^{\cos(3x)}$.

options.how_it_arises: Differentiated the innermost function $3x$ to $3$, but left the outer function $e^{\cos(3x)}$ undifferentiated.
options.feedback: You differentiated the innermost term $3x$ to $3$, but left $e^{\cos(3x)}$ undifferentiated. Differentiate the middle cosine layer as well to introduce the factor $-\sin(3x)$.
Correct! Working through each layer gives $e^{\cos(3x)} \cdot (-\sin(3x)) \cdot 3 = -3\sin(3x) e^{\cos(3x)}$.

questions.solution: Applying the chain rule across all three layers: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{du}[e^u] \cdot \frac{d}{dv}[\cos(v)] \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[3x]$ where $u = \cos(3x)$ and $v = 3x$. This gives $e^{\cos(3x)} \cdot (-\sin(3x)) \cdot 3 = -3\sin(3x) e^{\cos(3x)}$.
